title: Deepika Padukone Is Pregnant, Shooting Two Action Epics, and Still the Most Wanted Woman in Indian Cinema
excerpt: She announced a second baby in April, was back throwing punches on Shah Rukh Khan's King within 48 hours, and now Atlee is rewriting his Allu Arjun spectacle around her. The body double is the only one breaking a sweat.
body:
It takes a particular kind of star to announce a pregnancy and then, forty-eight hours later, walk onto a soundstage in Vile Parle and take on eight men in a fight sequence. Deepika Padukone is that kind of star.

When she and Ranveer Singh confirmed in April that baby number two was on the way, the internet did what the internet does — cooed, congratulated, and immediately started writing her off the year's biggest films. Surely she'd step back. Surely the action would be quietly handed to someone younger and hungrier. Trade circles buzzed with speculation about her commitments. Then the dates leaked, and the speculation curdled into something closer to awe: on April 21 and 22, barely two days after the announcement, Deepika was at Golden Tobacco Studio shooting a highly stylised combat set-piece for King, trading blows alongside Shah Rukh Khan against a swarm of eight fighters.

So much for stepping back.

"What keeps me balanced is just being truthful, authentic. Whenever I'm faced with complicated or difficult situations, to be able to listen to my inner voice and stand by decisions that give me peace — that's when I feel most in equilibrium." — Deepika Padukone, to Vogue Arabia in Stockholm
"On a ₹600-crore-plus canvas built across parallel universes, with Allu Arjun in his first-ever double role, the leading lady is the one piece nobody is willing to compromise."

That quote, delivered in a haze of Cartier diamonds at the unveiling of the maison's 'En Équilibre' high-jewellery collection, was meant to be about poise. Instead, Bollywood read it like a tarot card. The whisper networks decided she was sending a coded message about her very public exit from Sandeep Reddy Vanga's Prabhas-starrer Spirit — the project she walked away from amid reports of "unusual demands," after which Vanga took to social media to question, without quite naming her, the kind of person she is and the feminism she claims to stand for. Deepika, characteristically, named no one back. She just let the diamonds talk.

!Vogue Arabia — Photo: Wikimedia Commons

Here is the thing about being the most bankable woman in the industry: you don't have to win the argument. You only have to keep working. And the work is staggering.

The two-film juggling act

Director Atlee — the man who turned Jawan into a cultural earthquake — has reportedly torn up his own shooting plan to keep Deepika at the centre of his next, the sci-fi action spectacle tentatively known as Raka (a.k.a. AA22xA6), opposite Telugu phenomenon Allu Arjun. With roughly 50 shooting days left on her schedule, Atlee didn't recast or reduce her. He drafted a 'Plan B': a body double for the most punishing stunt work, while Deepika handles the close-ups, the drama, and that all-important entry sequence the makers are mounting like a coronation. Her character, by all accounts, stays fully intact — not a line trimmed, not a scene deleted. On a ₹600-crore-plus canvas built across parallel universes, with Allu Arjun in his first-ever double role, the leading lady is the one piece nobody is willing to compromise.

Over on King, Siddharth Anand's team performed the same calculus in reverse: fast-track her. Capture the action and song sequences early, while the pregnancy is in its gentlest weeks. After the Mumbai combat marathon comes a climax set-piece with the international unit in South Africa, followed by an elaborate sandy-backdrop sequence at a specialised studio in Mira Road. Her close-ups are already in the can; the stunt footage will be married to them later with VFX so seamless you'll never spot the join. King also carries the weight of history — it marks the big-screen debut of Suhana Khan opposite her father — and Deepika is woven through the spectacle as its glamorous, dangerous heart.

Why the diaspora should care

For NRIs in the US, UK and Canada, this is the rare year both of Deepika's tentpoles are being engineered for the global theatrical experience — King aimed at a worldwide release, Raka built in the pan-India mould that has been filling diaspora multiplexes from Edison to Hounslow. Expect day-one Friday shows, Telugu and Hindi versions running side by side, and the now-familiar ritual of opening-weekend whistles in suburban American cinemas.

There's something quietly radical in watching the industry's biggest female star refuse the old script — the one where pregnancy meant a polite disappearance. Deepika rewrote it into a flex. She's expecting, she's headlining the two most expensive films of her career, and she's letting a stunt double take the bruises while she takes the close-up. Unstoppable doesn't quite cover it.
